query: An equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi high-entropy alloy has a simple solid-solution structure and favorable plasticity and machinability but relatively low hardness and strength, while its microstructure and deformation behavior remain insufficiently understood. Under hardness testing and mechanical loading of this starting state, what single intervention could overcome the strength and hardness limitation while retaining its favorable mechanical characteristics? State the proposed intervention, its mechanism, the predicted measurable change relative to the unmodified alloy, its applicable processing and test conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a microstructural and mechanical experiment that could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The addition of a minor amount of boron (0.1 at.%) to the equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi high-entropy alloy can overcome the strength and hardness limitation while retaining its favorable mechanical characteristics.

generation.conditions: As-cast or annealed state, room temperature or elevated temperature testing
generation.structural_mediator: Intergranular precipitation of hexagonal close-packed borides
generation.mechanism: Grain boundary cohesion enhancement and work hardenability improvement due to boride precipitation, derived from materials-science principles and supported by records PMC9572892 and PMC5893566
generation.predicted_outcome: Increased hardness and strength, improved ductility and work hardenability, and reduced grain boundary brittleness

generation.boundary: 0.1 at.% boron addition, as-cast or annealed state, room temperature or elevated temperature testing
generation.uncertainty: The exact amount of boron addition and processing conditions required to achieve optimal mechanical properties, and the potential effects of boron addition on other properties such as corrosion resistance and magnetic behavior

falsification_experiment.design: Microstructural and mechanical characterization of the modified alloy with and without boron addition, using techniques such as X-ray diffraction, scanning electron microscopy, and tensile testing
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the addition of 0.1 at.% boron does not result in significant improvements in hardness, strength, and ductility, and/or does not lead to the expected intergranular precipitation of borides, then the hypothesis is falsified

Magnetically-driven phase transformation strengthening in high entropy alloys

Abstract: AbstractCrCoNi alloy exhibits a remarkable combination of strength and plastic deformation, even superior to the CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy. We connect the magnetic and mechanical properties of CrCoNi, via a magnetically tunable phase transformation. While both alloys crystallize as single-phase face-centered-cubic (fcc) solid solutions, we find a distinctly lower-energy phase in CrCoNi alloy with a hexagonal close-packed (hcp) structure. Comparing the magnetic configurations of CrCoNi with those of other equiatomic ternary derivatives of CrMnFeCoNi confirms that magnetically frustrated Mn eliminates the fcc-hcp energy difference. This highlights the unique combination of chemistry and magnetic properties in CrCoNi, leading to a fcc-hcp phase transformation that occurs only in this alloy, and is triggered by dislocation slip and interaction with internal boundaries. This phase transformation sets CrCoNi apart from the parent quinary, and its other equiatomic ternary derivatives, and provides a new way for increasing strength without compromising plastic deformation. Microstructure and Mechanical Properties of Intergranular Boride Precipitation-Toughened HfMoNbTaTiZr Refractory High-Entropy Alloy

Abstract: AbstractTo develop strong refractory high-entropy alloys for use at elevated temperatures as well as to overcome grain-boundary brittleness, an equimolar HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy was prepared, and a minor amount of boron (0.1 at.%) was added into the alloy. The microstructures of the alloys were characterized, and their macro-to-microscale mechanical properties were measured. The microstructural observations indicated that the matrices of both the alloys were composed of a body-centered cubic solid-solution structure, and the added boron induced the precipitation of hexagonal close-packed borides (most likely the (Hf, Zr)B2) at the grain boundaries. The modulus and hardness of differently oriented grains were about equivalent, suggesting a diminished anisotropy, and many small slips occurred on multiple {110} planes. While the hardness of the matrix was not increased, the intergranular precipitation of the borides markedly raised the hardness of the grain boundaries.
